title: ADONIJAH ASKED FOR ONE WOMAN—SOLOMON HEARD A CLAIM TO THE THRONE
paragraphs: ADONIJAH ASKED FOR ONE WOMAN—SOLOMON HEARD A CLAIM TO THE THRONE

It sounded like a marriage request. Solomon heard something far more dangerous. And buried inside this brutal story is a warning for every person who has ever surrendered something to God… only to quietly reach for it again.
There are requests that sound innocent until you know the history behind them.
There are sentences that seem harmless until you understand who is speaking.
And there are moments in Scripture when a few ordinary words carry the weight of a throne.
Adonijah walked toward Bathsheba after King David was dead.
He said he came in peace.
He spoke respectfully.
He acknowledged that Solomon possessed the kingdom.
Then he asked for one woman.
Abishag.
And almost immediately, Adonijah was a dead man.
If you read 1 Kings 2 too quickly, Solomon can seem shockingly severe. A man asks to marry a woman, and the king responds as though someone has attempted a coup.
But this story did not begin with Abishag.
It began with a throne.
And once you see that, the entire passage changes.
Before David died, Adonijah had already decided what he believed belonged to him.
Scripture introduces the problem with a chillingly simple statement:
"וַאֲדֹנִיָּה בֶן־חַגִּית מִתְנַשֵּׂא לֵאמֹר אֲנִי אֶמְלֹךְ"
Va’Adoniyyah ben-Chaggith mitnasse lemor, ani emlokh.
Adonijah son of Haggith was exalting himself, saying, in essence:
“I will be king.”
Those final Hebrew words are devastatingly revealing:
"אֲנִי אֶמְלֹךְ"
Ani emlokh.
“I will reign.”
That is the heartbeat beneath the story.
Not merely ambition.
Self-exaltation.
Adonijah did not begin by asking what God had appointed. He began with what Adonijah wanted.

He prepared chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. He gathered powerful allies, including Joab and Abiathar. He held a sacrificial feast and invited royal sons and influential supporters—but conspicuously excluded Solomon, Nathan, Zadok, Benaiah, and others connected with Solomon’s succession.
He was building the appearance of kingship before he possessed the throne.
And that should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because you do not need chariots to imitate Adonijah.
Sometimes we do it with careers.
Relationships.
Ministry.
Recognition.
Money.
Influence.
Platforms.
We pray, “Your will be done,” while quietly arranging fifty runners in front of the thing we already decided God should give us.
We call it faith.
Sometimes it is ambition wearing religious clothing.
We call it waiting on God.
Sometimes we are simply waiting for God to agree with us.
Adonijah wanted the throne.
But God’s purpose was moving elsewhere.
David publicly installed Solomon as king, and Adonijah’s attempted rise collapsed almost instantly.
Suddenly the people who had been celebrating with him scattered.
The man who had said, “I will be king,” found himself afraid of the king who actually sat on the throne.
Adonijah fled to the altar and grasped its horns, fearing Solomon would kill him.
And this is important.
Solomon did not immediately execute him.
He gave him an opportunity.
According to 1 Kings 1:52, Solomon essentially declared that if Adonijah proved himself worthy, he would live; if wickedness were found in him, he would die.
Mercy stood between Adonijah and judgment.
Remember that.
Because when we reach Abishag, we are not looking at an isolated request from an innocent stranger.
We are looking at a previously self-appointed rival to the throne who had been spared.
Then David died.
And Adonijah approached Bathsheba.
She saw him coming and asked the question that almost seems to hang over the entire conversation:
"הֲשָׁלוֹם בֹּאֶךָ"
Ha-shalom bo'ekha?
“Do you come in peace?”
Adonijah answered:
"שָׁלוֹם"
Shalom.
“Peace.”
But sometimes a person can speak peace while still carrying an unsurrendered ambition.
He began talking about the kingdom.
That alone matters.
He reminded Bathsheba that he had expected to reign and claimed Israel had looked toward him. Then he admitted that the kingdom had become Solomon’s because it was Solomon’s “from the LORD.”
Think about the contradiction.
Adonijah could recognize God’s sovereignty with his mouth while still making a request Solomon would interpret as threatening the kingdom God had established.
That is one of the most frightening forms of spiritual self-deception.
Knowing the right theology without surrendering the heart.
You can say God is sovereign…
and still resent His decision.
You can say Jesus is Lord…
and still negotiate over the rooms of your life He is allowed to enter.
You can sing surrender on Sunday…
then spend Monday trying to recover what you supposedly laid down.
Adonijah then made his request.
He wanted Abishag the Shunammite as his wife.
Who was Abishag?

When David became extremely old and could not keep warm, his servants searched Israel for a young woman to attend him. They found Abishag of Shunem. Scripture carefully tells us that she cared for David, but David did not sexually “know” her.
She had nevertheless belonged to the intimate setting of David’s royal household.
So when Adonijah—the older brother who had already attempted to become king—asked to receive the woman who had attended the former king, Solomon did not hear an ordinary romantic proposal.
He heard a political claim.
When Bathsheba presented the request, Solomon answered with words that expose how he understood it:
Why ask Abishag for Adonijah?
Ask the kingdom for him also.
That is the interpretive key Scripture itself gives us.

We should be careful not to claim more than the text tells us. Scripture does not give us a private confession from Adonijah saying, “I am using Abishag to launch another coup.” We therefore should not pretend to know every hidden motive in his heart.
But Scripture leaves no ambiguity about Solomon’s judgment of the request.
Solomon connected Abishag directly with the kingdom.
He also mentioned Adonijah’s previous political allies, Abiathar and Joab.
The request was therefore not treated as an isolated marriage proposal.
It landed inside an already dangerous struggle over royal succession.
And Solomon responded decisively.
Adonijah was executed.
It is a disturbing scene.
It should be.
The Bible does not sanitize the violent realities of ancient monarchy.

Nor should Christians turn Solomon’s action into permission for personal vengeance, coercion, violence, or cruelty today. This is descriptive history within Israel’s monarchy, not a command telling Christians to imitate royal executions.
Our King gave His Church a different weapon.
The Gospel.
The Word of God.
Truth.
Prayer.
Love.
And a cross.
Yet beneath the political drama lies a spiritual warning that reaches frighteningly close to home.
Adonijah lost the throne…
but apparently could not completely leave the throne alone.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Because there are things we surrender publicly while secretly keeping emotionally.
You said you gave God that relationship.
But you keep checking.
You said you forgave that person.
But you rehearse the wound every night.
You said you surrendered your future.
But panic consumes you whenever God's timetable disagrees with yours.
You said Jesus has your life.
But there is still one Abishag you keep asking for.
One doorway back.
One compromise.
One hidden conversation.
One secret appetite.
One piece of your former kingdom that you keep telling yourself is harmless.
“It’s only this.”
“It’s not really rebellion.”
“I’m not going back.”
“I just want one small thing.”
That phrase should terrify us.
Because enormous spiritual collapses often introduce themselves as small requests.
Sin rarely walks into your life announcing:
“I have come to destroy you.”
It whispers:
“Just this once.”
“Just one message.”
“Just one look.”
“Just one drink.”
“Just one lie.”
“Just one compromise.”
“Just one private habit nobody needs to know about.”
“Just one little piece of the old life.”
And slowly, quietly, the thing you buried starts breathing again.
This is why Jesus did not preach behavior modification.
He preached repentance.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια—metanoia—for repentance: a turning of mind and direction, not merely feeling embarrassed because consequences arrived.
The Gospel does not ask you to decorate your old throne.
It calls you down from it.
Jesus does not come merely to become one more adviser in the kingdom of your life.
He comes as King.
And here is where Adonijah's tragedy points us toward something infinitely greater than Solomon.
Solomon protected his throne by putting a rival to death.
Jesus Christ established His saving kingdom by giving His own life for His enemies.
That difference changes everything.
At Calvary, the rightful King was mocked as though He were a counterfeit king.
A crown of thorns was pressed onto His head.
A royal robe was thrown around Him in ridicule.
And above the crucified Christ appeared the accusation identifying Him as King of the Jews.
Human beings mocked His kingship while unknowingly standing before the King through whom forgiveness would be offered to rebels.
Adonijah said:
“I will be king.”
Humanity has been repeating that sentence since Eden.
Maybe not with our mouths.
But with our lives.
I will decide what is good.
I will decide what is evil.
I will decide what my body is for.
I will decide whom I will forgive.
I will decide what truth means.
I will decide what obedience costs.
I will decide how much of myself God gets.
Ani emlokh.
“I will reign.”
That is the ancient rebellion buried inside the modern heart.
And then Jesus comes.
Not merely saying, “Behave better.”
He says:
Follow Me.
Lose your life for My sake.
Take up your cross.
Repent and believe.
The Gospel is not God helping you become a more successful ruler of your private kingdom.
The Gospel is the death of the illusion that the throne ever belonged to you.
And strangely…
beautifully…
when you finally stop fighting Christ for the throne, you discover that His reign is not your destruction.
It is your rescue.
Because this King receives repentant rebels.
This King touches lepers.
This King welcomes prodigals.
This King forgives adulterers who repent.
This King restores failures.
This King eats with sinners.
This King searches for lost sheep.
This King carries a cross.
This King walks out of a tomb.
And this King can take the most scandalous chapter of your life and write grace across pages you thought could never be redeemed.
Maybe your scandal is visible.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still smile in photographs while something inside you is collapsing.
Maybe you lead worship while fighting a secret addiction.
Maybe you post Bible verses while bitterness is poisoning you.
Maybe you encourage everyone else while privately wondering whether God could still want you.
Maybe you have gone so far from Jesus that returning feels hypocritical.
Hear the Gospel.
Your hope is not that your past becomes less ugly.
Your hope is that Christ is more gracious than your sin is powerful.
Grace does not pretend rebellion never happened.
Grace tells the truth about rebellion and then points to a Savior whose blood is sufficient for repentant sinners.
The cross is where God refuses to call evil good…
and still makes a way for guilty people to come home.
That is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is the doorway home.
You do not have to keep protecting the little kingdom that is killing you.
You do not have to keep reaching for Abishag.
You do not have to keep resurrecting what Christ is calling you to bury.
You can surrender.
Today.
Not when you become cleaner.
Not when you finally feel spiritual.
Not after you fix everything.
Come to Christ honestly.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess the sin.
Drop the performance.
Stop negotiating.
Stop calling chains freedom simply because you chose them yourself.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again. Forgiveness is not purchased by your religious performance.
It is received by grace through faith in Christ.
That distinction matters enormously.
Supporting Gospel work should flow from gratitude to God, never become a payment to God.
So if this article helped you see Scripture more clearly, exposed something hidden, or reminded you that Jesus is still calling you home, don't let the conviction disappear when you close Facebook.
You do not have to explain your entire story.
Sometimes three honest words are where healing conversations begin.
And think of one person who needs this tonight.
Not fifty strangers.
One person.
The friend quietly drifting from Christ.
The believer fighting an addiction nobody sees.
The brother who thinks failure has disqualified him forever.
The woman carrying shame from a chapter she cannot rewrite.
Send this to them privately if their struggle is sensitive.
Because one day the temptation may return disguised as “one small request,” and you may need to remember:
Do not negotiate with what God called you to surrender.
It doesn't.
Not because sharing saves you.
It cannot.
Jesus saves.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting the spread of biblical truth, one practical way you can participate is by supporting, sharing, and helping Gospel-centered resources reach farther than they could otherwise reach.
Not as a religious badge.
As a seed.
Because somebody scrolling tonight may be smiling publicly while privately reaching again for the very thing that nearly destroyed them.
Somebody needs to discover that repentance is still possible.
Somebody needs to hear that grace has not run out.
Somebody needs to know that Jesus receives people who finally stop defending their rebellion and come home.
Adonijah's story ends with death.
But yours does not have to end where your rebellion began.
There is another King.
A greater Son of David.
A King wiser than Solomon.
A King whose throne cannot be stolen.
A King who died beneath a sign declaring His kingship and rose with death defeated beneath His feet.
His name is Jesus.
And maybe the most important question left by Adonijah's story is not whether you understand why Solomon considered Abishag politically dangerous.
Maybe the question is much closer.
What are you still reaching for after God told you to surrender it?
What old throne are you still circling?
What “small request” is secretly carrying a much larger rebellion?
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
There is mercy at His feet.
There is forgiveness in His blood.
There is resurrection after ruin.
There is grace after scandal.
And when Jesus takes the pen, your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence.
The throne you keep fighting to control may be the very thing keeping you from discovering the freedom of finally kneeling before the King who died to bring you home.
